summary:
Marswalk is a web app that helps astronauts plan, rehearse and carry out one walk (EVA) on Mars. Existing tools like Mars Trek show whole regions; a crew on a four-hour walk needs smaller answers: is this slope too steep in a suit, how long is the walk back to the rover from here, is a solar storm coming, where does the radio to the rover cut out.

We tested it on a real place: the slopes of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity is driving now. Our route, EVA-1, visits three science stops Curiosity really visited, including the boxwork ridges it studied in 2025, and each stop shows Curiosity's photo from that spot.

The app plans the route on NASA's 1 m HiRISE terrain model and checks it against 18 crew risks: oxygen, slope, rocks, daylight, cold shadows, radio, radiation and live NASA solar storm forecasts. You can rehearse the walk in 3D and follow it on a helmet-style display, including emergency drills where the rover drives out to rescue the crew. It covers the whole 36 × 40 km area of NASA's 1 m terrain and also works offline.
details:
What it does

Marswalk is a web app that helps a Mars crew plan, rehearse and carry out one walk (EVA). Existing tools like Mars Trek show whole regions; on a four-hour walk the crew needs smaller answers: is this slope too steep in a suit, how long is the walk back to the rover from here, is a solar storm coming, where does the radio to the rover cut out. We tested it on a real place: the slopes of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity is driving now.

How it works

- Plan: the crew places a rover and science stops. The app computes the fastest safe walking route on NASA's 1 m HiRISE terrain model and gives a GO / NO-GO verdict with the reason, checked against 18 crew risks (oxygen, slope, rocks, daylight, cold shadows, radio, radiation, solar storms).

- Rehearse: the route in 3D on real terrain, with Curiosity's own photos at each stop.

- Walk: a helmet-style display with direction, time left, walk-back time, radio link, a Sun-based bearing (Mars has no GPS and a compass does not work) and the tasks at each stop. Emergency drills (suit leak, injured partner, solar storm) plan the way home or the rover's drive-out to the crew.

- Under the hood: A* routing with a walking-speed model and a metabolic model (Minetti 2002, scaled to Mars gravity); a walk-back time map; real ridge shadows for any time of the sol; radio line of sight; NASA DONKI solar storm forecasts. It covers the whole 36 × 40 km area of NASA's 1 m terrain and works offline.

What we found on our test route (13 November): the verdict was NO-GO because DONKI forecast a solar storm reaching Mars; the app found the next safe start (sol 5074, 10:00 local time). A ridge blocks the radio for 9 minutes, and one portable relay fixes it.

Benefits and impact

One map that combines terrain, science targets, safety rules and live conditions for a specific walk, so a crew can decide on the spot without waiting 4 to 24 minutes for Earth. The same approach works anywhere with a 1 m terrain model, including the Moon for Artemis.

What makes it creative

The route is planned around the astronaut's body and suit, not just distance: oxygen use depends on climbing, the plan always keeps a way home, and the map tells the crew when NOT to go. Each science stop shows the real view Curiosity saw from that spot.

Factors we considered

Crew safety first (walk-back reserve, buddy rule, radiation shelter), no GPS or compass on Mars, radio blocked by terrain, communication delay with Earth, cold shadows, dust season, tired muscles after a long flight, and planetary protection at sites that may hold traces of past life.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Leaflet (map), three.js (3D), a service worker (offline), Netlify (hosting), Remotion (demo video).

Limits

Walking speed and oxygen numbers come from published formulas, not real suit tests. That is the first thing we would like to check.
